title: Grapes and raisins
why_this_matters: Grape and raisin ingestion can cause acute kidney injury in dogs, but recent series show much lower rates of injury than the early reports [1][2].

what_changes_from_human.point: Grapes and raisins are a kidney hazard for dogs, and tartaric acid is the proposed toxic principle [2][4].
Early case series overstated the risk: a 139-dog series found AKI in 6.7% of dogs with data and one death [1].

recognition: Vomiting is the most common early sign [1]. All 43 dogs in the early ASPCA series vomited [2].
In 15 dogs with grape or raisin toxicosis and severe AKI, 11 had marked forebrain, cerebellar or vestibular signs, unrelated to the degree of azotemia [3].
In dogs that developed renal failure, hypercalcemia and a raised calcium-phosphorus product were common, and extreme values were negative prognostic indicators [2].
management: In a 139-dog series, AKI prevalence was 6.7% (8 of 120 with data), 88% underwent gastrointestinal decontamination and 138 of 139 survived. The authors state the retrospective design prevents conclusions about the value of decontamination [1].
In the earlier 43-dog series of dogs that had already developed renal signs, 53% survived, and reduced urine output, ataxia or weakness predicted a negative outcome [2].
AKI was also reported after cream of tartar and tamarinds, supporting tartaric acid as the likely toxic component [4].
On limited evidence, dried grapes were not more likely than fresh grapes to cause AKI [5].
No specific antidote is established. Calcium carbonate and probenecid have been proposed, without clinical validation [6][7].

takeaway: Treat any confirmed grape or raisin ingestion as a possible kidney injury, decontaminate early, and hand the dog to a veterinarian who can monitor kidney values.
